title: Confidence Respects Risk: Information Is Not Mastery
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How confident are you, and how much respect do you have for what could go wrong?

groups.heading: A very thin line between confidence and your perception of risk

lines.text: I pointed to the author's words about two big corporations coming at him.
two multibillion Dollar corporation were coming at us with a dagger pointed at our heart.

A student said it is a good example of how our relationship with growing a business, debt and money comes into play. It is terrifying. But if you look at the projections, you can find confidence that it will get better.

I said the author has an overabundance of confidence. He believes it is real: he has shown it time and again, even in life and death situations. But there is a balance between confidence and being irrational about it.

I've met people who are very confident but irrational, I said. They aren't taking calculated risks, and then they over-leverage. I knew a real estate investor who owned a lot of apartments, and when the market crashed in 2008 he went bankrupt.
Your confidence cannot be disrespectful to the risks, I said. The minute you lose respect and lose that fear, and the ability to see the negative coming, that is key. It is a very thin line.

groups.heading: Speed of information is not mastery of information

lines.text: When is it too much risk, and when is it too little, I asked? If you take too little, you are probably not growing as fast as you should. Too much, and you have a chance of failing. Where is that line?
What we cannot do, I said, is not be accountable, not have defined goals, and lie to ourselves. That is the big one.

The speed of information today is abundant, I said. You scroll Instagram, Facebook, the news. We confuse the speed of information with mastery of information. We think because we are getting the speed, we are getting the mastery. We're not.

People think that if I listen to this guy talk about entrepreneurship enough, I'm going to absorb it, and it replaces the hard work and the internal structures. Wrong. Then they don't have the daily habits or the threshold of work ethic, and they lie to themselves.

A student pointed to the author's line about going up against two big companies, like a tiny country going up against two superpowers, and winning. I read on: at the time we were charging fifteen cents a month per subscriber for one service, but they were going to offer both of their channels for free.

Can you imagine the stress of that, I said? Today we just assume a subscription model was born out of the blue. It was not. The author was a big part of defining a business model that didn't exist before.
Where is your line between confidence and respect for the risk?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write how confident you are in your plan, from one to ten.
Write the risks you respect, the ones that could hurt you.
Write one place you may be over-leveraged.
Write what you read or watch for information, and what you actually master.
Write one daily habit that is mastery, not just information.

check.q: What did I say your confidence cannot be?
What did I say we confuse with mastery of information?
What three things did I say we cannot do?
choices: Not be accountable, not have defined goals, and lie to ourselves

recap: Confidence must respect the risk. Information is not mastery.
